_link.title: I can use the right-hand grip rule to determine the direction of the magnetic field around a current-carrying wire

toLevel2.question: In the right-hand grip rule, what does the thumb represent?
toLevel2.correct: The direction of conventional current flow
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The right thumb points in the direction of conventional current, and the curled fingers show the field direction.

distractors.answer: The direction of the magnetic field lines
distractors.explanation: The curled fingers show the field direction, not the thumb.

distractors.answer: The direction of electron flow in the wire
distractors.explanation: The thumb represents conventional current (positive flow), not electron flow.

distractors.answer: The direction of the force on the wire
distractors.explanation: The grip rule finds field direction, not force; force uses a different hand rule.

toLevel2.question: In the right-hand grip rule, what do the curled fingers represent?
toLevel2.correct: The direction of the magnetic field lines around the wire
toLevel2.correctExplanation: When the thumb points along the conventional current, the curled fingers wrap in the direction of the circular magnetic field.

distractors.answer: The direction of the conventional current through the wire
distractors.explanation: The thumb shows current direction; the fingers show the field direction.

distractors.answer: The direction of force on a nearby charged particle
distractors.explanation: The grip rule determines field direction, not force on a particle.

distractors.answer: The strength of the magnetic field around the wire
distractors.explanation: The fingers show field direction, not strength.

toLevel2.question: A wire carries conventional current upward. Using the right-hand grip rule, which way does the magnetic field circulate when viewed from above?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Point the right thumb upward (current direction); the fingers curl anticlockwise when viewed from above.

distractors.answer: Clockwise around the wire
distractors.explanation: With the thumb pointing up, the fingers curl anticlockwise from above, not clockwise.

distractors.answer: Straight outward from the wire in all directions
distractors.explanation: The field forms circular loops, not radial lines.

distractors.answer: Straight downward along the length of the wire
distractors.explanation: The field circles the wire; it does not run along it.

toLevel2.question: Which hand is used in the right-hand grip rule for finding magnetic field direction?
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The rule specifically requires the right hand. Using the left hand would give the wrong field direction.

distractors.answer: The left hand only
distractors.explanation: The rule is called the right-hand grip rule; the left hand gives the opposite direction.

distractors.answer: Either hand works equally well
distractors.explanation: Only the right hand gives the correct field direction for conventional current.

distractors.answer: No hand is needed at all
distractors.explanation: The physical gesture of gripping with the right hand is the basis of this rule.

toLevel2.question: A wire carries current into the page (shown as ✕). Using the right-hand grip rule, the magnetic field circulates in which direction?
toLevel2.correct: Clockwise when viewed from the front of the page
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Point the right thumb into the page; the fingers curl clockwise as seen from the front.

distractors.answer: Anticlockwise when viewed from the front of the page
distractors.explanation: With current into the page, the right-hand grip rule gives clockwise, not anticlockwise.

distractors.answer: Upward along the wire toward the top of the page
distractors.explanation: The field forms circles around the wire, not straight lines along it.

distractors.answer: Downward along the wire toward the bottom of the page
distractors.explanation: The field circulates around the wire; it does not run along the page.

toLevel2.question: The right-hand grip rule can be used regardless of the orientation of the current-carrying wire.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The rule works for any wire orientation — horizontal, vertical, or angled — as long as you point the thumb in the direction of conventional current.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: Students may think the rule only works for vertical wires, but it applies to any orientation.

toLevel2.question: Using the left hand instead of the right hand in the grip rule gives the same field direction.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: Using the left hand reverses the curl direction, giving the wrong magnetic field direction. Only the right hand gives the correct result.

distractors.answer: True
distractors.explanation: The left hand gives the opposite curl direction; the rule specifically requires the right hand.

toLevel2.question: In the right-hand grip rule, the {{blank:1}} points in the direction of conventional current and the curled {{blank:2}} show the field direction.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The right thumb aligns with the current, and the fingers curl in the direction of the circular magnetic field.

blank:1.explanation: The thumb points along the current; the fingers show the field.
The thumb, not the palm, indicates the current direction in the grip rule.

blank:2.explanation: The thumb shows current direction; the curled fingers show the field direction.
The curled fingers indicate the field direction, not the wrist.

toLevel2.question: For a wire with current flowing out of the page, the magnetic field circulates {{blank:1}} when viewed from the {{blank:2}}.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: With the right thumb pointing out of the page toward you, the fingers curl anticlockwise as viewed from the front.

blank:1.explanation: Current out of the page gives anticlockwise field when viewed from the front.
The field forms circular loops, not radial lines.

blank:2.explanation: The standard viewing perspective is from the front of the page.
Field circulation direction is described as viewed from the front, not the side.

toLevel2.question: The right-hand grip rule uses {{blank:1}} current, which flows from positive to {{blank:2}}.
toLevel2.correctExplanation: The rule is based on conventional current direction, which is defined as flowing from the positive terminal to the negative terminal.

blank:1.explanation: The rule uses conventional current, not electron current, which flows in the opposite direction.
The grip rule uses conventional current direction, not the concept of alternating current.

blank:2.explanation: Conventional current flows from positive to negative, not positive to positive.
Conventional current flows from positive to negative terminal.

toLevel3.question: Why does the right-hand grip rule use conventional current rather than electron flow?
toLevel3.correct: Conventional current is the standard reference direction used in physics for analysing circuits and fields
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Physics conventions are built around conventional current (positive to negative). The grip rule is consistent with this established framework.

distractors.answer: Electron flow is too slow to produce a magnetic field around the wire in practice
distractors.explanation: Drift velocity is slow, but electrons do produce the field; the rule uses conventional current by convention.

distractors.answer: Conventional current actually matches the physical direction electrons move through metal
distractors.explanation: Electrons flow opposite to conventional current; the rule uses conventional current as a consistent standard.

distractors.answer: The right-hand grip rule gives the same result regardless of which current direction you use
distractors.explanation: Using electron flow with the right hand would give the wrong field direction; you must use conventional current.

toLevel3.question: A wire carries current to the right along a table. Using the right-hand grip rule, what is the field direction at a point directly above the wire?
toLevel3.correct: The field points away from you at that position above the wire
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Point the right thumb to the right; above the wire the fingers curl away from you (into the page if facing the current).

distractors.answer: The field points toward you at that position above the wire
distractors.explanation: Above the wire with current to the right, the grip rule gives field away from you.

distractors.answer: The field points to the right along the direction of the current flow
distractors.explanation: The field is perpendicular to the current, not parallel to it.

distractors.answer: The field points straight upward away from the surface of the table
distractors.explanation: The field is tangent to the circular loops, not radially outward from the wire.

toLevel3.question: Why does reversing the current direction reverse the magnetic field direction around the wire?
toLevel3.correct: The thumb now points the opposite way, so the fingers curl in the opposite direction
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The grip rule links field direction to current direction. Reversing the thumb reverses the finger curl, and hence the field.

distractors.answer: Reversing current doubles the field strength, which makes it appear reversed to instruments
distractors.explanation: Reversing current changes direction, not strength; the field genuinely reverses.

distractors.answer: The magnetic field does not actually reverse; only the current direction changes inside
distractors.explanation: The field direction is directly determined by current direction and does reverse.

distractors.answer: Reversing current switches the rule from right hand to left hand automatically
distractors.explanation: The right hand is always used; reversing current means pointing the thumb the other way.

toLevel3.question: How does the right-hand grip rule help explain the field pattern around a wire carrying current out of the page?
toLevel3.correct: The thumb points out of the page, and the fingers curl anticlockwise, showing the field direction
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Pointing the right thumb toward you (out of the page) causes the fingers to curl anticlockwise, matching the circular field pattern.

distractors.answer: The thumb points into the page, and the fingers curl clockwise around the wire symbol
distractors.explanation: Current out of the page means the thumb points out, not in; the curl is anticlockwise.

distractors.answer: The rule cannot be applied when current goes out of the page toward the observer
distractors.explanation: The rule works for any current direction, including out of the page.

distractors.answer: The thumb points sideways, and the fingers point along the wire in both directions
distractors.explanation: The thumb points in the current direction (out of the page), and fingers curl around it.

toLevel3.question: What advantage does the right-hand grip rule have over memorising field directions for individual cases?
toLevel3.correct: It provides one consistent method that works for any current direction in any orientation
toLevel3.correctExplanation: Rather than memorising clockwise or anticlockwise for specific cases, the grip rule gives the correct answer for any situation.

distractors.answer: It only works for horizontal wires, so it simplifies those specific problems only
distractors.explanation: The rule works for any wire orientation, not just horizontal.

distractors.answer: It requires a calculator to apply, which reduces the chance of manual errors
distractors.explanation: The rule is a physical gesture requiring no calculation.

distractors.answer: It gives approximate results that are close enough for most physics problems only
distractors.explanation: The rule gives exact field directions, not approximations.

toLevel3.question: A student uses the right-hand grip rule and points their thumb downward. In which direction do the fingers curl when viewed from above?
toLevel3.correct: Clockwise, because the thumb points down and the fingers wrap accordingly
toLevel3.correctExplanation: With the thumb pointing down, viewing from above shows the fingers curling clockwise around the axis.

distractors.answer: Anticlockwise, because downward current always gives anticlockwise field patterns
distractors.explanation: Thumb down gives clockwise from above; anticlockwise would be for thumb up.

distractors.answer: The fingers do not curl when the thumb points downward in any orientation
distractors.explanation: The fingers always curl around the thumb direction regardless of orientation.

distractors.answer: Radially outward, because the field spreads away from a vertical wire naturally
distractors.explanation: The field forms circular loops; the fingers curl in a circle, not radially.

toLevel3.question: If you know the direction of the magnetic field around a wire, you can use the right-hand grip rule in reverse to find the current direction.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The rule works both ways: curl the fingers in the field direction, and the thumb points in the conventional current direction.

distractors.answer: False
distractors.explanation: The grip rule is reversible; knowing the field direction lets you determine the current direction.

toLevel3.question: When current flows into the page, the right-hand grip rule shows the field circulates {{blank:1}} as viewed from the {{blank:2}}.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: With the thumb into the page, the fingers curl clockwise when viewed from the front of the page.

blank:1.explanation: Current into the page gives clockwise field from the front; anticlockwise is for current out of the page.
The field forms circular loops, not radial lines.

blank:2.explanation: The conventional view is from the front; viewing from the back reverses the apparent rotation.
The circulation direction is described from the front of the page, not from the top.

toLevel3.question: Reversing the {{blank:1}} direction in a wire reverses the {{blank:2}} of the magnetic field around it, as predicted by the grip rule.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The grip rule directly links current direction to field direction; reversing one reverses the other.

blank:1.explanation: It is the current direction that determines field direction in the grip rule.
Resistance is a scalar; reversing current direction reverses the field.

blank:2.explanation: Reversing current reverses the field direction, not its strength.
DC current does not have a frequency; the field direction reverses.

toLevel3.question: The right-hand grip rule works for a wire at {{blank:1}} orientation, making it a {{blank:2}} method for finding field direction.
toLevel3.correctExplanation: The rule applies to horizontal, vertical, or angled wires — it is a universal tool for determining field direction.

blank:1.explanation: The rule works for any orientation, not just vertical.
The rule is not limited to horizontal wires; it works at any angle.

blank:2.explanation: The grip rule is universal, not limited; it works for all orientations.
The rule gives exact directions, not approximate ones.

toLevel4.question: A long wire runs vertically and carries conventional current downward. At a point directly to the east of the wire, what is the direction of the magnetic field?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Point the right thumb downward; at the east side of the wire the fingers curl from south to north, so the field points north.

distractors.answer: Toward the south
distractors.explanation: At the east side with current downward, the grip rule gives northward, not southward.

distractors.answer: Toward the east
distractors.explanation: The field is tangent to the circle, perpendicular to the radial direction; it does not point east.

distractors.answer: Straight downward
distractors.explanation: The field circles the wire; it does not run parallel to the current at that point.

toLevel4.question: A wire carries current to the left across a page. At a point directly below the wire, what does the right-hand grip rule predict for the field direction?
toLevel4.correct: Out of the page toward the viewer
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Point the right thumb to the left; below the wire the fingers curl out of the page.

distractors.answer: Into the page away from the viewer
distractors.explanation: Below the wire with current to the left, the fingers curl out of the page, not into it.

distractors.answer: To the left along the current direction
distractors.explanation: The field is perpendicular to the current; it does not run parallel to it.

distractors.answer: To the right opposite to the current direction
distractors.explanation: The field direction is tangent to circles around the wire, not along the wire.

toLevel4.question: Two parallel horizontal wires are viewed from above. Wire A carries current to the right and wire B carries current to the left. At a point between the wires, how do their fields compare?
toLevel4.correct: Both fields point in the same direction between the wires, reinforcing each other
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Using the grip rule: below wire A (current right) the field points into the page, and above wire B (current left) the field also points into the page. The fields add up.

distractors.answer: The fields point in opposite directions and completely cancel each other out
distractors.explanation: With opposite currents, the fields between the wires point the same way and reinforce.

distractors.answer: The fields are perpendicular to each other and produce a diagonal resultant
distractors.explanation: The fields are parallel and in the same direction between the wires.

distractors.answer: Only one wire produces a field; the other wire's field is blocked between them
distractors.explanation: Both wires produce fields that coexist and add together in the space between.

toLevel4.question: A wire carries current out of the page. A student uses the right-hand grip rule and determines the field is anticlockwise. The current is then reversed. What is the new field direction?
toLevel4.correct: Clockwise, because the reversed current reverses the finger curl direction
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Reversing the current means the thumb now points into the page; the fingers curl clockwise from the front.

distractors.answer: Still anticlockwise, because the field direction does not depend on current direction
distractors.explanation: Field direction is directly linked to current direction; reversing current reverses the field.

distractors.answer: The field disappears entirely when the current is reversed in the wire
distractors.explanation: The field does not disappear; it reverses direction.

distractors.answer: The field becomes radial instead of circular when current is reversed in the wire
distractors.explanation: The field remains circular; only its circulation direction reverses.

toLevel4.question: A wire runs north to south and carries current toward the north. At a point to the west of the wire, what is the field direction?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Point the right thumb north; at the west side the fingers curl upward, so the field points up.

distractors.answer: Straight downward toward the ground
distractors.explanation: At the west side with current north, the grip rule gives upward, not downward.

distractors.answer: Toward the north along the wire direction
distractors.explanation: The field is perpendicular to the wire at any point; it does not run along the wire.

distractors.answer: Toward the east across the wire position
distractors.explanation: The field is tangent to the circle; at the west side it points up, not east.

toLevel4.question: A student knows the magnetic field at a point near a wire circulates clockwise when viewed from above. Using the grip rule in reverse, what can they determine?
toLevel4.correct: The conventional current flows downward through the wire
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Curl the right fingers clockwise (from above); the thumb points downward, indicating the current direction.

distractors.answer: The conventional current flows upward through the wire
distractors.explanation: Upward current gives anticlockwise field from above; clockwise means downward current.

distractors.answer: The wire carries no current at the moment of observation
distractors.explanation: A circulating field means current is flowing; the grip rule identifies its direction.

distractors.answer: The current direction cannot be found from the field direction alone
distractors.explanation: The grip rule works in reverse; field direction uniquely determines current direction.

toLevel4.question: A horizontal wire carries current toward the east. At a point directly above the wire, the field points in which direction?
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Point the right thumb east; above the wire the fingers curl from south to north. The field at that point is northward.

distractors.answer: Toward the south
distractors.explanation: Above the wire with current east, the grip rule gives northward, not southward.

distractors.answer: Toward the east
distractors.explanation: The field is perpendicular to the current at each point, not parallel.

distractors.answer: Straight upward
distractors.explanation: The field is tangent to the circular loops, not radially outward from the wire.

toLevel4.question: For current flowing to the right, the field above the wire points {{blank:1}} and the field below the wire points {{blank:2}}.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: With thumb right, above the wire fingers curl away from you (into page) and below they curl toward you (out of page).

blank:1.explanation: Above the wire with current to the right, the field points away from you.
The field is perpendicular to the current, not along it.

blank:2.explanation: Below the wire the field points toward you when current flows to the right.
The field is tangent to circles around the wire, not along the wire.

toLevel4.question: To use the grip rule in reverse, curl the right fingers in the {{blank:1}} direction and the thumb indicates the {{blank:2}} direction.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: Curling the fingers along the known field direction causes the thumb to point in the direction of conventional current.

blank:1.explanation: In reverse use, you curl fingers along the field direction to find the current.
The grip rule relates field and current, not force.

blank:2.explanation: The thumb gives the current direction when the rule is used in reverse.
The grip rule determines current direction from field direction, not force.

toLevel4.question: When a wire carries current into the page (✕), the field at the top of the wire points to the {{blank:1}} and at the bottom points to the {{blank:2}}.
toLevel4.correctExplanation: With thumb into the page, the clockwise curl means the field goes left at the top and right at the bottom.

blank:1.explanation: At the top of a wire with current into the page, the field points left, not right.
The field is tangent to circles; at the top it is horizontal (left), not vertical.

blank:2.explanation: At the bottom of the wire the field points right, not left.
The field at the bottom is horizontal (right), not downward.

toLevel5.question: A wire passes through the centre of a horizontal compass. Current flows north through the wire. Using the grip rule, at the position of the compass needle (to the east of the wire), what direction does the field point?
toLevel5.correct: Upward, which would tilt the north end of the needle upward if it were free to rotate in 3D
toLevel5.correctExplanation: With thumb pointing north, at the east side the fingers curl upward. The horizontal compass needle cannot follow this vertical field, limiting the visible deflection.

distractors.answer: Toward the east, causing the compass to point directly east from its position
distractors.explanation: The field at the east side is vertical (upward), not horizontal toward the east.

distractors.answer: Toward the north, reinforcing the compass needle's natural orientation completely
distractors.explanation: The field is upward at the east side, not northward.

distractors.answer: Downward, which would pull the south end of the needle downward from its rest
distractors.explanation: At the east side with current north, the field points upward, not downward.

toLevel5.question: Two vertical wires are side by side, both carrying current upward. At a point between the two wires, what can be said about their combined magnetic fields?
toLevel5.correct: The fields point in opposite directions and partially cancel between the two wires
toLevel5.correctExplanation: For wire on the left (current up), the field to its right points into the page. For wire on the right (current up), the field to its left points out of the page. These oppose and partially cancel.

distractors.answer: The fields point in the same direction and reinforce each other between the wires
distractors.explanation: With same-direction currents, the fields oppose between the wires, not reinforce.

distractors.answer: Only one wire's field exists between them because the closer wire dominates entirely
distractors.explanation: Both fields exist; they superpose and partially cancel.

distractors.answer: The fields are perpendicular to each other and create a diagonal resultant field
distractors.explanation: The fields are antiparallel (opposite directions) between the wires, not perpendicular.

toLevel5.question: A student applies the right-hand grip rule to electron flow instead of conventional current and gets an anticlockwise field. The actual conventional current gives a clockwise field. Analyse the student's error.
toLevel5.correct: Electron flow is opposite to conventional current, so the thumb pointed the wrong way
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The grip rule uses conventional current. Electrons flow opposite to conventional current, so using electron flow reverses the thumb direction and gives the wrong field direction.

distractors.answer: The student should have used the left hand for electron flow to get the right answer
distractors.explanation: While the left hand with electron flow gives the correct result, the standard approach is right hand with conventional current.

distractors.answer: The error is that electrons do not produce magnetic fields, only positive charges create them
distractors.explanation: Electrons do produce magnetic fields; the error is using the wrong current convention with the right hand.

distractors.answer: There is no error; both anticlockwise and clockwise are equally valid field directions
distractors.explanation: Only one direction is physically correct; the student's reversed answer is wrong.

toLevel5.question: Consider a wire carrying current to the right. At four compass points around the wire (above, below, left, right), how does the field direction change?
toLevel5.correct: The field direction rotates smoothly around the wire, pointing in a different direction at each position
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The circular field lines mean the tangent direction is different at every point around the wire: into page above, out below, up on left, down on right.

distractors.answer: The field points in the same direction at all four positions around the wire
distractors.explanation: The field is tangent to circles; it points in a different direction at each position.

distractors.answer: The field alternates between two opposite directions on opposite sides of the wire
distractors.explanation: The field rotates continuously; it does not simply alternate between two directions.

distractors.answer: The field is zero at the left and right positions and nonzero only above and below
distractors.explanation: The field exists at all positions around the wire; it is not zero anywhere nearby.

toLevel5.question: A wire carries current into the page. A second wire directly above it carries current out of the page. At the midpoint between the wires, how do the magnetic fields from each wire combine?
toLevel5.correct: Both fields point to the left at the midpoint, so they reinforce each other
toLevel5.correctExplanation: For the lower wire (current in), the field above it points left. For the upper wire (current out), the field below it also points left. The fields add.

distractors.answer: The fields point in opposite directions at the midpoint and completely cancel out
distractors.explanation: With opposite currents in this geometry, the fields at the midpoint are in the same direction.

distractors.answer: Both fields point to the right at the midpoint, reinforcing in that direction
distractors.explanation: Using the grip rule, both fields point left, not right, at the midpoint.

distractors.answer: One field points up and the other down at the midpoint, creating a vertical resultant
distractors.explanation: Both fields are horizontal (left) at the midpoint; they do not point vertically.

toLevel5.question: Why is the right-hand grip rule a consequence of the cross product relationship between current direction and magnetic field?
toLevel5.correct: The cross product inherently produces a result perpendicular to both inputs, matching the perpendicular circular field
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The Biot-Savart law involves a cross product (dl × r̂), which naturally produces a field perpendicular to the current. The right-hand grip rule is a physical representation of this mathematical operation.

distractors.answer: The cross product produces parallel results, and the grip rule compensates for this deficiency
distractors.explanation: The cross product produces perpendicular results, which the grip rule directly represents.

distractors.answer: The cross product is unrelated to the grip rule, which is just a memorisation trick only
distractors.explanation: The grip rule is a direct physical representation of the cross product in the Biot-Savart law.

distractors.answer: The cross product only works in two dimensions, so the grip rule extends it to three
distractors.explanation: The cross product is inherently three-dimensional; the grip rule represents it physically.

toLevel5.question: A wire carries current upward through a horizontal sheet of cardboard. Iron filings sprinkled on the cardboard form concentric circles. Using the grip rule, predict how a small compass on the cardboard would orient.
toLevel5.correct: The compass aligns tangent to the circles, pointing anticlockwise at its location
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The grip rule with thumb up gives anticlockwise field (viewed from above). The compass aligns tangent to the field lines in the anticlockwise direction.

distractors.answer: The compass points directly toward the wire at the centre of the circle pattern
distractors.explanation: The compass aligns tangent to the circles, not radially toward the wire.

distractors.answer: The compass points directly away from the wire in a radial outward direction
distractors.explanation: The field is tangential to the circles, not radial.

distractors.answer: The compass spins continuously because the field keeps changing around the wire
distractors.explanation: The field is steady; the compass settles in the tangent direction at its position.

toLevel5.question: Evaluate whether the right-hand grip rule could be replaced by a left-hand grip rule if electron flow were used as the reference direction.
toLevel5.correct: Yes — using the left hand with electron flow gives the same field direction as the right hand with conventional current
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Since electron flow is opposite to conventional current, using the opposite hand compensates and gives the correct field direction.

distractors.answer: No — the left hand always gives the wrong answer regardless of which current convention is used
distractors.explanation: The left hand with electron flow gives the same result as the right hand with conventional current.

distractors.answer: Yes — but only for wires oriented vertically, not for horizontal or angled wires at all
distractors.explanation: The substitution works for all orientations, not just vertical.

distractors.answer: No — electron flow and conventional current point in the same direction in all cases
distractors.explanation: Electron flow is opposite to conventional current, which is why the hand must also change.

toLevel5.question: The right-hand grip rule is a physical representation of the {{blank:1}} product in the Biot-Savart {{blank:2}}.
toLevel5.correctExplanation: The Biot-Savart law uses a cross product (dl × r̂) to calculate the magnetic field, and the grip rule physically demonstrates this relationship.

blank:1.explanation: The dot product gives a scalar; the cross product gives the perpendicular field direction.
A scalar product cannot produce a perpendicular direction; the cross product does.

blank:2.explanation: While it is an equation, the standard name is the Biot-Savart law.
It is known as the Biot-Savart law, not the Biot-Savart theorem.

toLevel5.question: Using electron flow with the {{blank:1}} hand gives the same magnetic field direction as using conventional current with the {{blank:2}} hand.
toLevel5.correctExplanation: Since electron flow is opposite to conventional current, the opposite hand compensates: left hand with electron flow equals right hand with conventional current.

blank:1.explanation: Using the right hand with electron flow gives the wrong field direction; the left hand is needed.
Only the left hand gives the correct result when using electron flow.

blank:2.explanation: The standard rule uses the right hand with conventional current, not the left.
Only the right hand gives the correct result with conventional current.
